{{Short description|Type of gravity anomaly}}
In [[geodesy]] and [[geophysics]], the '''Bouguer anomaly''' (named after [[Pierre Bouguer]]) is a [[gravity anomaly]], corrected for the height at which it is measured and the attraction of terrain.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Introduction to Potential Fields: Gravity |journal=U.S. Geological Survey Fact Sheets |date=1997 |volume=FS–239–95 |bibcode=1997usgs.rept...19W |url=https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/fs-0239-95/fs-0239-95.pdf |accessdate=30 May 2019 |last1=Water Resources Division |first1=U. S. Geological Survey |series=Fact Sheet |page=19 |doi=10.3133/fs23995 }}</ref> The height correction alone gives a [[free-air gravity anomaly]].

[[Image:Nj cboug.jpg|thumb|right|Bouguer anomaly map of the state of [[New Jersey]] (USGS)]]

==Definition==
The Bouguer anomaly <math>g_B</math> defined as:

<math display="block"> g_B = g_{F} - \delta g_B + \delta g_T </math>

Here, 
* <math>g_F</math> is the free-air gravity anomaly.
* <math>\delta g_B</math> is the ''Bouguer correction'' which allows for the gravitational attraction of rocks between the measurement point and sea level;
* <math>\delta g_T</math> is a ''terrain correction'' which allows for deviations of the surface from an infinite horizontal plane

The free-air anomaly <math>g_F</math>, in its turn, is related to the observed gravity <math>g_{obs}</math> as follows:

<math display="block"> g_F = g_{obs} - g_\lambda + \delta g_F</math>

where:
* <math>g_\lambda</math> is the correction for latitude (because the Earth is not a perfect sphere; see [[normal gravity]]);
* <math>\delta g_F</math> is the [[free-air correction]].

==Reduction==
A '''Bouguer reduction''' is called ''simple'' (or ''incomplete'') if the terrain is approximated by an infinite flat plate called the '''Bouguer plate'''. A ''refined'' (or ''complete'') Bouguer reduction removes the effects of [[terrain]] more precisely. The difference between the two is called the ''(residual) terrain effect'' (or ''(residual) terrain correction'') and is due to the differential gravitational effect of the unevenness of the terrain; it is always negative.<ref name=Hofmann>{{harvnb|Hofmann-Wellenhof|Moritz|2006|loc=Section 3.4}}</ref>

===Simple reduction===
The gravitational acceleration <math>g</math> outside a Bouguer plate is perpendicular to the plate and towards it, with magnitude ''2πG'' times the mass per unit area, where <math>G</math> is the [[gravitational constant]]. It is independent of the distance to the plate (as can be proven most simply with [[Gauss's law for gravity]], but can also be proven directly with [[Newton's law of universal gravitation|Newton's law of gravity]]). The value of <math>G</math> is {{val|6.67|e=-11|u=N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>−2</sup>}}, so <math>g</math> is {{val|4.191|e=-10|u=N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>−2</sup>}} times the mass per unit area. Using {{val|1|ul=Gal}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{val|0.01|u=m s<sup>−2</sup>}} ({{val|1|u=cm s<sup>−2</sup>}}) we get {{val|4.191|e=-5|u=mGal m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>−1</sup>}} times the mass per unit area. For mean [[Rock (geology)|rock]] [[density]] ({{val|2.67|u=g cm<sup>−3</sup>}}) this gives {{val|0.1119|u=mGal m<sup>−1</sup>}}

The Bouguer reduction for a Bouguer plate of thickness <math>H</math> is
<math display="block"> \delta g_B = 2\pi\rho G H </math>
where <math>\rho</math> is the density of the material and <math>G</math> is the constant of gravitation.<ref name=Hofmann/>  On Earth the effect on gravity of elevation is 0.3086&nbsp;mGal&nbsp;m<sup>−1</sup> decrease when going up, minus the gravity of the Bouguer plate, giving the ''Bouguer gradient'' of 0.1967&nbsp;mGal&nbsp;m<sup>−1</sup>.

More generally, for a [[mass distribution]] with the density depending on one Cartesian coordinate ''z'' only, gravity for any ''z'' is 2π''G'' times the difference in mass per unit area on either side of this ''z'' value. A combination of two parallel infinite if equal mass per unit area plates does not produce any gravity between them.
